 entertainment Patrick Stewart, legendary actor of Star Trek and X-Men fame, dies at 86
 Patrick Stewart poses in his dressing room at the Lyceum Theater in New York on Tuesday, April 1, 2008, where he is starring in a production of Macbeth. PHOTO: Associated Press file PUBLISHED ON October 30, 2026 12:50 AM Patrick Stewart, the classically trained actor who added Shakespearean gravitas to the Star Trek and X-Men franchises, has died. He was 86.
 Stewart died Wednesday in Los Angeles, following "a brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy Body Dementia, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said. Stewart's diagnoses had not been previously disclosed.
 "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today," Hugh Jackman, a frequent Stewart co-star in the X-Men universe, said on social media. "And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days."
 While best known as Professor Charles Xavier and Captain Jean-Luc Picard from the X-Men and Star Trek: The Next Generation series and films, respectively, Stewart spent more of his career onstage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise.
 Besides playing everyone from Claudius to Macbeth, he often performed a one-man rendition of A Christmas Carol and did West End and Broadway runs of Harold Pinter's No Man's Land and Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot in repertory with buddy Ian McKellen.
 He won three Olivier Awards, including one for playing Claudius in Hamlet opposite David Tennant. And he had a Grammy - in 1996 for best spoken word album for his recording of Peter and the Wolf.
 He achieved some of the best reviews of his career when he finally tackled Macbeth for the first time. The production, under the direction of Rupert Goold, debuted in May 2007 at England's Chichester Festival Theatre, switched to London's West End and then moved to the Brooklyn Academy of Music before transferring to Broadway in 2008.
 Stewart's performance earned him his sole Tony Award nomination. The Times of London said his Macbeth was "an enthralling creation of frailty, appetite, egotism and grim humour." The Daily Telegraph said he had turned in "a truly great performance" and The New York Times said it was "a must-see."
 "Nearly 50 years I've waited," Stewart told The Associated Press in 2008. "I learned it when I was 14. I memorized all the soliloquies just because I thought they were great. And they stuck, so I didn't have to learn those bits of the play, which is a blessing, because learning lines has now become the one curse of this job."
 Starship commander grew up without a toilet
 Raised in Mirfield in Yorkshire, a working-class corner of northern England, the future 24th-century commander of a starship grew up without a bathroom in his house.
 Stewart joined an amateur drama group at 12 and memorized Shakespeare for fun as a teen. He won a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, launching a career as a character actor.
 He had been bald since he was 19 - alopecia runs in his family.
 His father, a former regimental sergeant major in the British Army, was prone to outbursts of "repeated violence against my mother," as Stewart wrote in a newspaper piece. "Violence is always a choice a man makes and he alone is responsible for it."
 In his memoir, "Making It So," Stewart wrote about how he and his older brother Trevor braced for the nights when their dad came home drunk and angry, and attacked their mother. "Sometimes it was with an open hand, other times a closed fist. Always he aimed for her head."
 The son would later become a patron for Refuge, an organisation that provides shelter for domestic abuse victims.
 Loving Shakespeare proved fruitful as Captain Picard
 "The stage would prove to be a safe space, a refuge from real life in which I could inhabit another person, living in another place and time," he would write.
 Stewart was accepted into the Royal Shakespeare Company and stayed for 14 years, playing everything from Mark Antony to Henry IV to Shylock to Oberon. "People who were not in the company would say to me, 'Give it a break. Why don't you go somewhere else?' And I would say, 'To do what?'" he told the AP. "Telly?"
 Stewart eventually left to look for more varied work, including the 1981 film Excalibur. He had just done a production of Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? in 1987 when an interesting offer came along. "I found myself in Hollywood shooting a syndicated science fiction series, which I was assured would fail."
 It didn't, of course. Thanks to Stewart's rich baritone and noble bearing, the Star Trek franchise ran for seven years, 178 episodes and produced four feature films. He was known for his slogan Make it so.
 His adoration for Shakespeare would serve him well when he began to play Jean-Luc Picard, a 24th century starship commander.
 "There is a formality to the way they speak and comport themselves that remind me of numerous Shakespearean situations I'd been in onstage. I should play Jean Luc, I realised, as if he were a character in 'Henry IV,' which is about brave men," Stewart wrote in his memoir.
 Despite the Borg and Klingons, Stewart still managed to make room for blank verse. He established the Paramount Shakespeare Company, a workshop on Saturday and Sunday mornings for any actor interested. (Stewart revisited Picard in the TV series Star Trek: Picard.)
 Stewart died just a few days after Walter Koenig, another Star Trek icon, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov on the original NBC TV show from 1966 to 1969.
 "What a heartbreaking week it has been," William Shatner, who played Captain James T. Kirk in the franchise, wrote on Instagram. "Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did."
 Star Trek: The Next Generation gave him higher visibility, which led to more work, including roles in the films Conspiracy Theory, L.A. Story and on Broadway, where he starred in The Tempest, The Caretaker and David Mamet's A Life in the Theater. He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in June 2010. Stewart was also an ambassador for the International Rescue Committee.
 A brave and commanding persona. But sexy?
 In July 1992, he and supermodel Cindy Crawford were on the cover of TV Guide's "Top Turn-Ons," based on a readers' poll. In his memoir, Stewart wrote: "Absurd."
 Stewart was first introduced as the character Xavier in the original X-Men trilogy, appearing in three films from 2000 to 2006. He later returned in four more movies before Professor X's death in 2017's Logan. He reappeared in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness in 2022 and reprised the role in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday.
 He also showed off his comedic chops aboard Seth MacFarlane's Starz show Blunt Talk for two series and voiced Poop in The Emoji Movie. He made appearances on Robot Chicken, Futurama and The Simpsons (in one episode, Homer loses his hair, and Stewart tells him it's great to be bald.) One of his last credits was with Jackman in 2026's The Sheep Detectives.
 Later in life, he proved internet-savvy and found new fans with his humour, posing in a bath in a lobster suit and triggering memes when he posted a photo of him picking apples. When he was mistakenly outed as gay by a British newspaper, he said it was a nice change. "At least I didn't wake up to the internet telling me I was dead again," he tweeted.
 He married Brooklyn songwriter and singer Sunny Ozell in 2013, with the actor's X-Men co-star McKellen officiating. Stewart later tweeted a photo of the newlyweds in a ball pit.
 He is also survived by two children, a daughter, Sophia, and a son, Daniel.
